content: Inhaled corticosteroids are available in a suspension form for nebulisation, but the role of this delivery method in managing chronic asthma remains uncertain. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of inhaled corticosteroids delivered via nebulisers compared to those delivered using a holding chamber for the treatment of chronic asthma. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed using the Cochrane Airways Group Trial Register and reference lists of relevant articles. The authors of studies and pharmaceutical companies were also contacted to identify additional studies. The last search was conducted in January 2008. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing nebulisers to holding chambers for delivering inhaled corticosteroids in patients with chronic asthma were included. Studies involving patients of all age groups were considered. Two reviewers independently assessed the articles for inclusion and evaluated the methodological quality of the included studies. Data extraction was performed by one reviewer, and any missing information was clarified by contacting the study authors. Quantitative analyses were conducted using Review Manager 4.1 software. Two studies involving a total of 63 adult participants were included in the review. Additionally, a small study involving 14 children was identified during the 2005 update. The methodological quality of the included studies varied, and due to differences in study design, pooling the results was not appropriate. One high-quality study compared the use of budesonide at doses ranging from 2000 to 8000 mcg delivered via a Pari Inhalier Boy jet nebuliser with inspiration-only inhalation to budesonide 1600 mcg delivered via a large-volume spacer. The results showed that nebuliser delivery was associated with higher morning peak expiratory flow (PEF) values (an increase of 25 L/min, p < 0.01) and higher evening PEF values (an increase of 30 L/min, p < 0.01). Additionally, the nebuliser group demonstrated reduced use of rescue beta2-agonists and lower symptom scores compared to the holding chamber group. The authors concluded that high-dose budesonide delivered via the specific nebuliser used in the only double-blinded study included in this review was more effective than budesonide 1600 mcg delivered via a large-volume spacer. However, it remains unclear whether this difference was due to the nominal dose delivered or the delivery system itself. Factors such as cost, patient compliance, and individual preferences are critical determinants of clinical effectiveness and require further investigation. Future research is necessary to assess the relative effectiveness of inhaled corticosteroids delivered by various nebuliser/compressor combinations compared to holding chambers. Additionally, further studies are needed to evaluate these delivery methods in infants and preschool-aged children, as these populations are more likely to be considered for treatment with nebulised corticosteroids.
